title: The Law of Sines
short: Sides are proportional to the sines of their opposite angles.
trouble: Students pair a side with an angle that is not opposite it.

blocks.html: Right-triangle trig needs a right angle. For any triangle, the area formula from Triangle Area with Sine gives a relationship between sides and angles that works every time. We use the usual labels: side $a$ is opposite $\angle A$, side $b$ opposite $\angle B$, side $c$ opposite $\angle C$.

The area of $\triangle ABC$ can be written three ways, using each angle: $\frac{1}{2}bc \sin A = \frac{1}{2}ac \sin B = \frac{1}{2}ab \sin C$. Divide all three by $\frac{1}{2}abc$: $\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}$. Flip each fraction to get the usual form.

Law of Sines: $$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}.$$ Each side is paired with the sine of the angle across from it. Use it when you know two angles and a side (AAS or ASA), or two sides and an angle opposite one of them.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag the corners and read the sides and angles. Divide any side by the sine of the angle across from it: all three quotients agree.

blocks.title: Two angles and a side
blocks.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 40^\circ$, $m\angle B = 65^\circ$ and $a = 12$. Find $b$ and $c$ to the nearest tenth.

blocks.title: An exact answer
blocks.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 30^\circ$, $m\angle B = 45^\circ$ and $a = 6$. Find $b$ exactly.

blocks.title: Finding an angle
blocks.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 70^\circ$, $a = 20$ and $b = 14$. Find $m\angle B$.
steps: Since $b < a$, $\angle B$ must be smaller than $\angle A$, so this acute answer is the only one.

blocks.html: When you know two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA) and the side opposite the known angle is the shorter one, there can be two possible triangles. That is the same SSA trouble you met with congruence. If the side opposite the known angle is the longer one, as in the last example, there is only one.

Pairing a side with an angle that is not opposite it, such as $\frac{a}{\sin B}$. Each fraction must hold a side and the angle across from it. Check with the letters: lowercase $a$ goes with capital $A$.
